title: Navneet Kaur's Journey From a Cricket-Loving Home to India's Hockey World Cup Spark
excerpt: The Haryana forward, named Player of the Tournament at the FIH World Cup Qualifiers, draws inspiration from Indian cricket's global success as she eyes a podium finish.
body:
• Navneet Kaur scored a hat-trick at the FIH World Cup 2026 Qualifiers and was named Player of the Tournament, helping India secure qualification.
  • The forward from Shahabad Markanda, Haryana, chose hockey over cricket despite her father's wishes — there was no cricket infrastructure in her hometown.
  • India's heartbreaking fourth-place finish at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics continues to drive the team's ambitions for a podium finish at the World Cup and LA 2028.

In a small town in Haryana where hockey sticks outnumber cricket bats, Navneet Kaur found the sport that would define her life. The Indian women's hockey forward has emerged as one of the team's most dangerous attackers ahead of the FIH Hockey World Cup later this year, and her path to the national squad began with an unlikely detour from her family's first love.

A Father's Dream, a Daughter's Choice

Navneet grew up in Shahabad Markanda, a region in Haryana's Kurukshetra district that has produced a disproportionate number of India's hockey internationals. Her father, who worked in a TV repair shop, wanted her to become a cricketer. But cricket infrastructure simply did not exist in Shahabad.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=KBi-mWiMQrI

"My father wanted me to be a cricketer, but there was no cricket in my hometown. There was a school in front of my house where hockey was played and that's where I started playing the sport."

— Navneet Kaur, speaking on Hockey India's Hockey Te Charcha podcast

Her father pivoted, channeling his energy into supporting her hockey career instead. "My father, who used to work in a TV repair shop, has put in a lot of effort to help me reach the Indian team," Navneet said on the podcast, according to Sportskeeda.

Rising Through the Ranks

Navneet's breakthrough came early. She was part of the Indian junior team at the 2013 Hockey Junior World Cup, where India won a bronze medal after a dramatic shoot-out — in which Navneet herself scored. Several players from that junior squad went on to form the core of the senior national team.

https://x.com/TheHockeyIndia/status/2089251480784212125

"A lot of players from that Indian Junior team are playing together in the current Senior India Team. It has felt really nice to play with the same players for so many years," she told Hockey Te Charcha.

Her rise through the senior ranks came through years of sacrifice. "There were difficult days," Navneet admitted to Olympics.com. "Being away from family, pushing yourself every day — it's not easy. But I never thought of giving up. Hockey gave me happiness, and that kept me going."

Tokyo's Heartbreak, World Cup Redemption

The defining moment in Indian women's hockey came at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, where the team reached the semifinals and finished fourth — agonizingly close to a medal. For Navneet and her teammates, the near-miss left a lasting mark.

"We were so close, and that feeling stays with you," she reflected, according to Olympics.com. "It pushes you during training, during matches, during the toughest moments. We don't want to miss out again."

That hunger was on full display at the FIH World Cup 2026 Qualifiers, where Navneet delivered a standout performance. She scored a hat-trick — the only player in the tournament to do so — and was named Player of the Tournament. Her goals played a crucial role in India finishing as runners-up and securing their spot at the World Cup later this year, according to Livemint.

Cricket's Triumph as Fuel

Navneet has drawn particular motivation from the Indian women's cricket team's World Cup victory under Harmanpreet Kaur. She sees it as a paradigm shift for Indian women's sport.

"Seeing Harmanpreet Kaur and the Indian women's cricket team lift the World Cup tells us what is possible," she told Olympics.com. "It gives us the belief that we can achieve the same in hockey."

"When you see an Indian team win at that level, it changes your mindset," she added. "You stop hoping and start believing. That is what we want as a team — to go all the way."

What's Next

Now a senior leader in the squad, Navneet has taken on a mentoring role alongside her attacking duties. "As a senior, I feel responsible for the younger players," she said. "I try to share my experiences and help them settle in. When everyone grows together, the team becomes stronger."

Her goals are clear: a podium finish at the FIH Hockey World Cup and a medal at the LA 2028 Olympics. For a forward who chose hockey over cricket in a town where the sport was all there was, the stage has never been bigger.
